title: The Jerusalem Council: Grace for the Gentiles
summary: Teachers from Judea tell the Gentile believers at Antioch that they cannot be saved unless they are circumcised, and the church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem to settle the question. After Peter, Barnabas, Paul, and James speak, the apostles and elders agree that Gentiles are saved through grace and need not be circumcised or keep the law of Moses, and they send a letter asking only that Gentile believers avoid four practices. Afterward Paul and Barnabas disagree sharply over John Mark and go separate ways.
story: Everything since Cornelius has been building to this chapter. Peter's vision, the church at Antioch, and the first missionary trip have brought large numbers of Gentiles into the church, and now the question can no longer be avoided: must these Gentiles become Jews, marked by circumcision and bound to the whole law of Moses, in order to belong to Israel's Messiah? The chapter sits almost exactly at the center of Acts, and its answer shapes the rest of the book and of church history. After the council, Peter leaves the story, James presides in Jerusalem, and Paul, now with Silas, sets out on a second trip that will carry the gospel into Europe.
historical:
The council probably met around AD 48 or 49. That date comes from working backward from Paul's arrival in Corinth, which the Gallio inscription at Delphi helps fix near AD 50-51 (Gallio was proconsul of Achaia about AD 51-52). The James who speaks decisively here is not the apostle killed in chapter 12 but James the brother of Jesus, who led the Jerusalem church until he was killed in AD 62, as Josephus reports.

Paul describes a visit to Jerusalem in Galatians 2:1-10, and how that visit relates to Acts 15 is one of the classic puzzles of the New Testament. Many scholars identify the two: the same people (Paul, Barnabas, Peter, James, John) discuss the same issue (whether Gentile believers must be circumcised) and reach the same result (they need not be). On this view the differences, such as Paul's emphasis on a private meeting and his silence about the letter of verses 23-29, reflect his purpose in Galatians, where he is defending his independence from Jerusalem's authority. Other scholars identify Galatians 2 with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30. They note that in Galatians Paul is carefully listing every contact he had with Jerusalem, and Acts 11 would be his second visit, as Galatians 2 is; that the request to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10) fits a relief visit; and that if the council had already ruled, Paul could simply have cited its decision against his opponents. On this reading Galatians was written just before the council and is Paul's earliest letter. Both views are held by careful scholars, and neither changes the council's outcome.
cultural:
Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17) and, for Jews of this period, the defining mark of belonging to Israel, alongside Sabbath and food laws. Gentiles who converted fully to Judaism (proselytes) were circumcised. The believers from the party of the Pharisees (verse 5) reasoned from Scripture: if Gentiles were joining Israel's Messiah, they should join Israel in the way the law prescribed. Their position was serious and sincere, not merely narrow.

The four requests in the council's letter (to avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, meat of strangled animals, and sexual immorality) have been understood in several ways. Many see them as drawn from Leviticus 17 and 18, which laid certain rules on foreigners living among Israel, so that Gentile believers could share a table and a community with Jewish believers without giving offense. Others emphasize that each item was associated with pagan temple worship, where sacrificed meat, blood, and sexual rites often went together. Some ancient manuscripts omit strangled animals and add a form of the golden rule, turning the list into a purely moral one. James's closing reason (Moses is read in every synagogue) suggests that sensitivity to Jewish neighbors is part of the point.
literary: The chapter is built as a report of a deliberative assembly: a problem (verses 1-5), a meeting (verse 6), speeches (verses 7-21), a decision and a letter (verses 22-29), and its reception (verses 30-35). Three witnesses speak in turn. Peter argues from experience (God gave the Spirit to Gentiles), Barnabas and Paul from signs and wonders, and James from Scripture, quoting Amos 9:11-12 in a form close to the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), which reads that the remnant of men may seek the Lord where the Hebrew speaks of possessing the remnant of Edom. The letter itself is a formal Greek letter with greeting and farewell. The chapter closes with an honest coda (verses 36-41): the same leaders who reached agreement on the gospel could not agree about a colleague.

outline.t: The dispute at Antioch reaches Jerusalem
Peter: saved through grace, just as they are
Barnabas and Paul report signs among the Gentiles

doctrines.note: Peter's conclusion is the heart of the chapter: we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are (verse 11). Jews and Gentiles are saved in the same way, by grace received through faith, and God cleansed their hearts by faith, not by circumcision.

The council does not declare the law of Moses worthless; Jewish believers continued to keep it. It decides that the law is not the way Gentiles enter God's people, and it asks for practices that make shared life between Jewish and Gentile believers possible.

The church settles its first great doctrinal dispute by gathering, listening to testimony, testing it by Scripture, and reaching a common decision that seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Later church councils looked to this as a pattern.

words.note: Zugos, yoke, the wooden frame laid across the necks of working animals. Jewish teachers could speak positively of taking up the yoke of the law. Peter uses the image of a burden too heavy to carry, not to despise the law but to confess that neither we nor our fathers kept it well enough to be saved by it. Jesus offered his own yoke as easy (Matthew 11:29-30).

Kardiognostes, heart-knower, a word used in the New Testament only here and in Acts 1:24. God, who knows the heart, judged the Gentiles' faith real and proved it by giving them the Spirit. What people cannot verify by outward marks, God sees directly.

Skene, tent or tabernacle. In Amos the fallen tent of David pictures the ruined house of David's dynasty. James reads its rebuilding as fulfilled in the risen Son of David gathering a people that includes Gentiles, which is why Gentiles need not first become Jews.

christ: The council's decision is a confession about Christ. If circumcision and law-keeping were required for Gentiles, then belonging to Jesus would not be enough; one would need Jesus plus Moses. Peter's answer is that the grace of the Lord Jesus saves Jew and Gentile alike. James adds that in Jesus, the Son of David, God has rebuilt David's fallen house, so that Gentiles may seek the Lord and be called by his name as Gentiles. The chapter thus shows what it means that Christ is the fulfillment of the law and the promises: those promises always included the nations, and Christ is now gathering them. The Gentile believers' freedom is not a lowering of standards but a recognition of how much Christ has done.

hard.q: Do the council's requirements, such as abstaining from blood and strangled meat, still bind Christians?
hard.a:
Most Christian traditions have not treated the food requirements as permanent law. They note that Paul, who delivered the council's decisions (16:4), later taught that food offered to idols could be eaten with a clear conscience unless it harmed a weaker believer or involved participation in idol worship (1 Corinthians 8 and 10), and that the requirements aimed at fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers in a particular setting. On this view the principle endures (do not use your freedom in a way that wounds others or compromises with idolatry), while the specific food rules served their time.

Others read the requirements more permanently. Some Christian communities, such as the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, have long kept food rules drawn from the Old Testament, and some interpreters argue that since the requirements rest on laws given to all peoples living among Israel, they carry abiding weight. The prohibition of sexual immorality, by contrast, is repeated throughout the New Testament and is treated by all traditions as permanent. The question of the food laws is second-order, and Christians have held both views in good conscience.

questions: The believers from the party of the Pharisees argued sincerely from Scripture. How can a church disagree seriously about something important without treating the other side as enemies?
Peter confessed that neither the apostles nor their ancestors had managed to bear the law's yoke. What yokes do Christians still place on newcomers today?
Paul and Barnabas agreed about the gospel but could not agree about Mark. What does that honest ending teach about unity and disagreement in the church?
